segments.text: Alright, look, it's inevitable.
Some of the most dangerous materials you're going to encounter are going to happen in
a laboratory setting.
In its laboratory safety guidance, OSHA does establish some basic safety standards that
every employer has to provide.
Here's one.
Employers shall furnish to each of his employees employment and a place of employment which
are free from recognized hazards that are causing or likely to cause death or serious
physical harm to his employees.
What's this mean?
This means keeping your workplace free, clear, and clean of any dangerous or recognized hazards.
In our case, we're focused on explosive materials, chemicals, and dangerous pathogens.
Manufacturers are required to furnish laboratories with SDSs, or Safety Data Sheets.
This sheet should have information that every employee will need to know to maintain the
laboratory safely.
This is going to include the chemical name, manufacturer info, hazardous components and
identity information, physical and chemical characteristics, fire and explosion hazard
data, reactivity data, health hazard data, precautions for safe handling and use, and
also control measures.
SDSs are really your go-to document for laboratory material safety.
If you understand that a material, for example, has an explosion hazard, then that's going
to activate a new set of guidelines.
OSHA recommends conducting a Process Hazard Analysis, or PHA, on any hazardous chemicals,
including chemicals that can be explosively reactive with other chemicals.
One policy here to maintain a safe and effective lab is to invite a PHA team with knowledge
of the explosive materials and evaluate any potential causes and consequences of fires and
explosions.
The PHA relating to explosives and pyrotechnics may include such topics like inherent chemical
and physical properties of specific explosives or explosive compounds, quantity distance requirements,
building design, human factors, and prior incident reports.
